pests.name: Birds
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ripe and near-ripe berries disappear, half-eaten fruit and purple droppings appear on the ground and on nearby surfaces, and flocks work the tree through the ripening weeks. On a large tree the loss is simply shared; on a small or netted tree it can be nearly total if not managed.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Birds strip the ripe berries fast. You will see missing fruit, half-eaten berries, and purple bird droppings under and around the tree. Big flocks can show up daily while the fruit ripens.
pests.cause_seasoned: Many birds, especially catbirds, mockingbirds, robins, and waxwings, are drawn to sweet, soft mulberries and feed heavily as they ripen. This is the number-one reason home growers lose fruit, and it is a feature as much as a pest, since a mulberry is one of the best wildlife trees you can plant.
pests.cause_beginner: Lots of birds love sweet, soft mulberries and eat them as they ripen. This is the main reason people lose fruit to the tree, though it is also why a mulberry is such a great tree for attracting birds.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: For a small tree, drape bird netting over it as the first berries color, and harvest ripe fruit promptly each day so less hangs available. For a large tree, netting is impractical; the traditional answer is to plant enough that there is plenty to share, and some growers deliberately keep a mulberry as a decoy to lure birds away from cherries and other prized fruit.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: For a small tree, cover it with bird netting when the first berries start to color, and pick ripe fruit every day so there is less left for the birds. A big tree is too large to net, so the usual approach is to accept that you are sharing, or even to let the mulberry act as a decoy that keeps birds off your other fruit.
pests.prevention_seasoned: There is no way to keep birds off a large mulberry, so plan the siting and the crop around sharing: a big tree yields far more than a household can use. Net only small or dwarf trees, and pick promptly.
pests.prevention_beginner: You cannot really keep birds off a big mulberry, so plan on sharing; luckily the tree makes far more fruit than you can eat. Only bother netting small or dwarf trees, and pick ripe fruit quickly.

pests.name: Whiteflies
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny white flying insects lift off the undersides of leaves when disturbed, sometimes with sticky honeydew and sooty mold on lower foliage in a heavy infestation. Vigor is rarely affected on an established tree.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny white flies rise up off the undersides of the leaves when you brush the branches, sometimes leaving a sticky film and black sooty mold below. They rarely bother an established tree much.
pests.cause_seasoned: Whiteflies (including the mulberry whitefly) are sap-feeders that colonize leaf undersides. They are a common but minor mulberry pest and mostly a cosmetic nuisance.
pests.cause_beginner: Whiteflies are small sap-sucking insects that gather under the leaves. They show up on mulberry fairly often but rarely do real harm.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: A healthy tree needs no treatment. If numbers are high on a small tree, a strong water spray to the leaf undersides or an insecticidal-soap application knocks them back; encourage the lacewings and ladybugs that prey on them.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: A healthy tree does not need treatment. On a small tree with a lot of them, spray the undersides of the leaves with a strong jet of water or insecticidal soap, and welcome the ladybugs and lacewings that eat them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep the tree vigorous and avoid heavy nitrogen feeding, which encourages the soft growth whiteflies favor. Natural predators usually keep them in balance outdoors.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the tree healthy and go easy on nitrogen feeding, which draws whiteflies. Natural predators usually keep them under control outside.

pests.name: Borers
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small entry holes, frass, or oozing on the trunk and larger limbs, usually on trees already stressed by drought, injury, or decline. Healthy, vigorous mulberries are seldom attacked.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Small holes, sawdust-like frass, or oozing on the trunk or big branches, mostly on trees that are already stressed or damaged. A healthy tree is rarely bothered.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several wood-boring beetle and moth larvae can attack mulberry, but almost always as a secondary problem on trees weakened by drought stress, mechanical wounds, or age. Borers follow decline rather than cause it in a healthy tree.
pests.cause_beginner: A few kinds of borer (beetle and moth larvae) can get into mulberry, but usually only when the tree is already weak from drought, wounds, or old age. They tend to follow trouble rather than start it.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: The durable control is tree health: water through droughts, avoid trunk wounds from mowers and trimmers, and prune out and destroy any dead or infested wood. There is no practical rescue spray for larvae already tunneling inside.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: The best fix is a healthy tree: water it in droughts, keep mowers and trimmers off the trunk, and cut out and destroy any dead or infested branches. Once larvae are inside the wood, no spray reaches them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep the tree vigorous and unwounded. A well-sited, adequately watered mulberry rarely gives borers an opening.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the tree healthy and avoid wounding the trunk. A well-placed, watered mulberry rarely has borer trouble.

diseases.name: Popcorn disease
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Some berries on the tree swell up abnormally, with individual segments (carpels) enlarging and staying hard and greenish, so the fruit looks like a little cluster of popcorn kernels instead of a normal soft berry. Affected fruit does not ripen properly and clings to the tree.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Some berries grow oddly, with the little segments puffing up hard and greenish so the fruit looks like tiny popcorn instead of a soft berry. Those berries never ripen right and hang on the tree.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Popcorn disease is caused by the fungus Ciboria carunculoides, which infects the developing fruit and turns the carpels into hard sclerotia. It is largely a southern problem, and white mulberries and their hybrids are the most susceptible; it is usually of minor importance but can cause real fruit loss on trees grown for eating.
diseases.cause_beginner: Popcorn disease is a fungus (Ciboria carunculoides) that gets into the developing fruit and makes it swell into hard, popcorn-like lumps. It mostly shows up in the South, and white mulberries and hybrids catch it most. It is usually minor but can cost you fruit on a tree you grow for eating.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no home spray that cures it. Control is sanitation: as the disease appears, remove and destroy the affected fruit on the tree and rake up and bury or discard fallen fruit and debris beneath it, since that is where the fungus overwinters to reinfect next year.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: No home spray fixes it. The control is cleanup: pick off and throw away the affected berries, and rake up and bury or bin the fallen fruit under the tree, because that is where the fungus waits out the winter to come back next year.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Year-round sanitation is the prevention: clear fallen and mummified fruit each season so the fungus has nowhere to overwinter. Where popcorn disease is a known local problem, favor red mulberry or a more resistant hybrid over the most susceptible white types.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep the ground under the tree clean of fallen fruit each year so the fungus cannot overwinter. If popcorn disease is common in your area, choose a red mulberry or a tougher hybrid rather than the most susceptible white types.

diseases.name: Bacterial blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Angular, water-soaked spots appear on the leaves and turn dark, and young shoots can show black streaks or stripes; badly hit shoot tips may die back. Damage is usually cosmetic on an established tree and worst in wet springs.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Leaves get angular, water-soaked spots that turn dark, and new shoots can have black streaks; bad cases kill the shoot tips. It usually just looks bad rather than harming an established tree, and it is worst in wet weather.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Bacterial blight is caused by the bacterium Pseudomonas syringae pv. mori, which spreads in cool, wet spring weather and enters young tissue. It is a minor mulberry disease that flares in wet seasons and rarely threatens a healthy tree.
diseases.cause_beginner: Bacterial blight is a bacterium (Pseudomonas syringae pv. mori) that spreads in cool, wet spring weather and infects new growth. It is a minor disease that shows up in wet years and rarely hurts a healthy tree.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out and destroy blackened, blighted shoots during dry weather to remove the bacterial source, and avoid overhead watering that keeps foliage wet. No spray is warranted on a home tree beyond this sanitation.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut out and throw away the blackened, blighted shoots in dry weather, and avoid watering over the top of the tree so the leaves stay drier. On a backyard tree, that cleanup is all that is needed.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Keep the canopy open and the foliage dry, prune only in dry weather, and remove infected wood promptly. A vigorous, well-spaced tree shrugs off the disease in most years.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep the tree open so air moves through it, prune only when it is dry, and remove any infected shoots. A healthy, well-spaced tree easily shrugs this off most years.

diseases.name: Leaf spots and minor foliar diseases
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Scattered fungal leaf spots, or whitish patches (false mildew and powdery mildew) on leaf undersides in mid to late summer, sometimes with modest leaf drop on older trees in a wet season. Vigor and cropping are rarely affected.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Spots on the leaves, or whitish patches underneath them in late summer, sometimes with a few leaves dropping in a wet year. It rarely affects how the tree grows or fruits.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A group of minor leaf fungi (Cercospora and Cercosporella leaf spots, false mildew, and powdery mildews) can spot or coat mulberry foliage, mostly late in the season and mostly in wet weather. On mulberry these are cosmetic and seldom worth treating.
diseases.cause_beginner: A few minor leaf fungi (leaf spots and mildews) can mark mulberry leaves, mostly late in the season and in wet weather. On mulberry they are just cosmetic and rarely worth doing anything about.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No treatment is needed on a healthy tree. Rake and remove fallen leaves in autumn to reduce carryover, and keep the canopy open for airflow. Fungicides are reserved for prized specimens with a serious recurring problem.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: A healthy tree needs no treatment. Rake up and remove fallen leaves in fall to cut down on next year's spores, and keep the tree open so air flows through. Sprays are only for special trees with a bad, repeated problem.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Open-canopy pruning, autumn leaf cleanup, and good air movement are the whole prevention program. Well-grown mulberries carry these diseases without meaningful harm.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keeping the tree open, cleaning up fallen leaves in fall, and letting air move through are all you need. A well-grown mulberry carries these without real harm.

pests.name: Pawpaw peduncle borer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Open flowers wilt, blacken, and drop just as they should be setting fruit. Splitting a dropped flower reveals a small pale caterpillar tunneling in the fleshy flower stalk (the peduncle) and floral tissue. In a bad year the borer can destroy the majority of a tree's blossoms, so a heavy bloom yields almost no fruit.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Flowers wilt, turn black, and fall off right when they should be turning into fruit. If you open a fallen flower you may find a tiny pale caterpillar tunneling inside the flower stalk. In a bad year it can ruin most of the flowers, so a tree that bloomed heavily still gives you very few pawpaws.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of the pawpaw peduncle borer (Talponia plummeriana), a small moth. At roughly 5 millimeters the larva is easy to miss, and the feeding happens out of sight inside the flower itself, so the first sign is a bloom that dies back and drops instead of setting fruit. How much of the bloom you lose swings widely from one season to the next.
pests.cause_beginner: The caterpillar of a small moth called the pawpaw peduncle borer. It burrows into the soft tissue of the flower, which makes the flower die and fall. How bad it is changes a lot from one year to the next.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no practical spray for a backyard tree once larvae are inside the flowers. The workable response is sanitation: gather and destroy dropped, infested flowers to reduce the local population, and lean on hand pollination of the healthy flowers to secure a crop despite the losses. Damage is rarely fatal to the tree and often eases the following year.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no easy spray for this on a home tree once the caterpillars are inside the flowers. The best thing you can do is pick up and throw away the fallen, damaged flowers to lower their numbers, and hand-pollinate the healthy flowers so you still get fruit. It does not hurt the tree itself, and it is usually less of a problem the next year.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep the ground under the tree clear of fallen flowers and debris where the borer can complete its cycle. A tree with two genetic partners and hand pollination will still set a crop from the flowers the borer misses, so protecting fruit set is more about pollination insurance than eradication.
pests.prevention_beginner: Rake up and remove fallen flowers so the borer cannot keep its cycle going under the tree. Because pawpaw already sets fruit unreliably, the best insurance is to hand-pollinate the good flowers so you get fruit from the ones the borer does not reach.

pests.name: Zebra swallowtail caterpillars
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Chewed young leaves, usually only a few at a time, with a green-and-black banded caterpillar feeding on the foliage. Damage is almost always light and cosmetic; the caterpillars never appear in numbers large enough to defoliate a tree.
pests.symptoms_beginner: A few young leaves chewed here and there, with a striped green-and-black caterpillar on them. The damage is minor and just cosmetic; there are never enough of them to strip a tree.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of the zebra swallowtail butterfly (Protographium marcellus), for which pawpaw is the sole larval host plant. The caterpillars feed only on young pawpaw foliage and never in great numbers, so they are far more a delight than a threat: the striking adult butterfly depends entirely on pawpaw.
pests.cause_beginner: The caterpillar of the zebra swallowtail butterfly, which can only grow on pawpaw leaves. It feeds on the young leaves but never in big numbers. This is really a bonus, not a pest problem: the beautiful butterfly needs pawpaw to survive.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: No treatment is warranted. The feeding is negligible, and controlling it would remove the caterpillars of a native butterfly that has no other host. Simply leave them be.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Do nothing. The leaf nibbling is harmless, and these are the caterpillars of a lovely native butterfly that has nowhere else to live. Just enjoy them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: None needed or advised. A healthy pawpaw shrugs off the light feeding, and the butterfly is a welcome part of having the tree.
pests.prevention_beginner: None needed. A healthy pawpaw is not bothered by them, and the butterfly is one of the nicest reasons to grow the tree.

pests.name: Fruit-raiding wildlife (raccoons, opossums, squirrels)
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ripe and nearly ripe fruit disappears from the tree or is found half-eaten on the ground, often overnight, right as it softens. Because pawpaw ripens over a short window and soft fruit is highly aromatic, animals frequently harvest it before the gardener does.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Ripe or almost-ripe fruit vanishes from the tree or turns up chewed on the ground, usually overnight, just as it gets soft. The strong ripe smell draws animals, and they often get to the fruit before you do.
pests.cause_seasoned: Raccoons, opossums, squirrels, and other wildlife are strongly attracted to the intense aroma of ripening pawpaw. Deer, by contrast, avoid the foliage and fruit, so the competition here is from fruit-eating mammals, not browsers.
pests.cause_beginner: Raccoons, opossums, squirrels, and other animals love the strong smell of ripening pawpaw and will help themselves. Deer are the exception: they avoid pawpaw leaves and fruit, so it is the fruit-eaters you are competing with.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Beat the animals to the fruit: pick pawpaws firm but full-sized as they begin to soften and finish ripening indoors, rather than leaving tree-ripe fruit hanging overnight. Check the tree daily through the harvest window. Netting or trunk baffles help where pressure is heavy.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Get to the fruit first. Pick pawpaws when they are full-sized and just beginning to soften, then let them finish ripening indoors instead of leaving soft fruit on the tree overnight. Check the tree every day while it is ripening. Netting or a baffle on the trunk can help if animals are a big problem.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Harvest promptly and do not let ripe fruit accumulate on the tree or ground. Since pawpaw is so perishable anyway, picking at the first give and ripening indoors both protects the crop from wildlife and gives you better control over the fruit.
pests.prevention_beginner: Pick fruit promptly and do not let ripe pawpaws pile up on the tree or the ground. Since the fruit does not keep long anyway, picking it as soon as it starts to soften and ripening it indoors both saves it from animals and lets you manage it better.

diseases.name: Phyllosticta leaf and fruit spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small tan-to-brown spots on the leaves and, at times, superficial dark blotches on the fruit skin. The spotting is cosmetic: it does not defoliate a healthy tree or spoil the flesh, and the fruit inside remains sound. Worst in warm, wet, humid summers with crowded, poorly ventilated foliage.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small tan or brown spots on the leaves, and sometimes dark surface blotches on the fruit skin. It looks worse than it is: the spots are just on the surface, do not harm the tree, and the fruit inside is fine. It shows up most in warm, wet, muggy summers.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fungi in the Phyllosticta group (and similar leaf-spot fungi). Spores spread in warm, humid, wet weather, and infection is favored by dense canopies that stay wet. Pawpaw is otherwise notably free of serious disease.
diseases.cause_beginner: A leaf-spot fungus that spreads in warm, damp weather, especially where leaves stay wet and crowded. Apart from this minor spotting, pawpaw has very few disease problems.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No fungicide is warranted for what is a cosmetic issue. Improve airflow by not crowding trees, rake and remove fallen spotted leaves at season's end to reduce carryover, and keep the tree vigorous. The fruit is unaffected inside and fully edible.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: No spray is needed for what is only a cosmetic problem. Give trees room for air to move, rake up and remove the spotted fallen leaves in autumn, and keep the tree healthy. The fruit itself is fine to eat.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space and site trees for good air movement, avoid overhead wetting of the foliage, and clear fallen leaves in autumn. These reduce the minor spotting; no routine spray program is needed for pawpaw.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Give trees enough space for air to move, avoid wetting the leaves when you water, and clean up fallen leaves in fall. That keeps the minor spotting down. Pawpaw does not need a regular spray schedule.

pests.name: Codling moth
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Larvae tunnel into the fruit core, leaving a frass-filled entry hole (often at the calyx end) and brown trails; infested Asian pears drop early or are inedible.
pests.symptoms_beginner: This is the classic 'worm in the fruit.' You find a small hole with brown crumbly stuff (frass) around it, and a tunnel into the core when you cut it open. Bad pears drop early.
pests.cause_seasoned: Cydia pomonella; female moths lay eggs on developing fruit and young leaves near bloom, and hatching larvae bore into the pear. Two or more generations per season in most regions. The same pest attacks apple.
pests.cause_beginner: A small moth lays eggs on the tiny pears in spring; the eggs hatch into caterpillars that crawl into the fruit. There can be two batches a summer, so the problem repeats.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Monitor with pheromone traps to time control; remove and destroy dropped and infested fruit; bag individual fruit; spinosad or kaolin clay on a degree-day/petal-fall schedule. Mating disruption works at larger scale.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick up and throw away every pear that drops, do not leave them under the tree. You can slip paper bags over young pears to keep moths out, and scent traps help you know when to act. Sprays like spinosad work if timed right.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Orchard sanitation (clear dropped fruit and debris), keep nearby abandoned pear or apple trees pruned or removed, and band trunks to catch larvae seeking pupation sites.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the ground under the tree clean of fallen pears, and wrap a band of cardboard around the trunk to trap crawling caterpillars. Nearby neglected pear or apple trees make it worse.

pests.name: Pear psylla
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Nymphs feed in clusters on shoots and leaves and exude copious sticky honeydew that blackens with sooty mold; heavy feeding causes leaf scorch, premature drop, fruit russeting, and tree decline. The signature pear pest.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves and young pears get coated in a sticky, shiny film that turns black and grimy (sooty mold), and the leaves may scorch and drop. Tiny insects cluster on the new shoots.
pests.cause_seasoned: Cacopsylla pyricola; a small psyllid specific to pear that overwinters as an adult and builds several overlapping generations through the season. Outbreaks follow broad-spectrum sprays that kill its natural enemies.
pests.cause_beginner: A tiny pear-specific insect (a kind of jumping plant louse) that sucks sap and oozes sticky stuff. It can build up fast, especially if bug sprays have wiped out the good bugs that normally keep it down.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dormant-season horticultural oil to smother overwintering adults and eggs; in-season insecticidal soap or summer oil; conserve natural enemies (anthocorid bugs, lacewings) by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides; kaolin clay deters egg-laying.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray horticultural oil while the tree is dormant in late winter to smother the overwintering insects, and use insecticidal soap in the growing season. Avoid harsh sprays, which kill the helpful bugs that eat psylla.
pests.prevention_seasoned: A well-timed dormant oil program plus a natural-enemy-friendly spray regime is the backbone of psylla management; avoid the lush nitrogen-pushed growth psylla favors.
pests.prevention_beginner: A good dormant oil spray in late winter and going easy on harsh sprays and fertilizer keep this pear-specific pest in check.

pests.name: Stink bug
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Stink bugs, including the invasive brown marmorated stink bug, pierce developing fruit to feed, leaving dimpled, catfaced pears with hard, corky, pithy brown patches in the flesh under each feeding site. The skin often looks nearly normal while the interior is pitted. Worst near weedy field and woodland borders.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Stink bugs poke the growing pears to feed, leaving dented, lumpy fruit with hard brown corky spots inside. The outside can look mostly fine while the flesh underneath is pitted and dry.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several native stink bugs plus the invasive brown marmorated stink bug (Halyomorpha halys); adults and nymphs feed on fruit from petal fall through harvest, moving in from surrounding weeds, crops, and woodland edges.
pests.cause_beginner: Shield-shaped bugs, including an invasive kind called the brown marmorated stink bug, that suck on the fruit through the season. They move in from nearby weeds, fields, and woods.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Kaolin clay deters feeding; clear weedy and brushy borders that harbor them; hand-pick or trap adults; bagging individual fruit excludes them. Where pressure is high, use a labeled product timed to nymph emergence and conserve natural enemies.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Coating the fruit with kaolin clay (a fine white clay spray) helps keep them off, and clearing weeds and brush around the tree removes their hideouts. You can also slip bags over young fruit to protect them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Cut back weedy borders and brush piles, monitor with traps from bloom on, and bag fruit where damage recurs. Avoid broad-spectrum sprays so predators keep populations down.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the area around the tree tidy, since weeds and brush are where they live, watch for them from bloom onward, and bag the fruit if they are a yearly problem.

pests.name: Pear scab
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Olive-green to black velvety spots on leaves, shoots, and fruit; fruit lesions become corky and cracked, and severe infection causes leaf yellowing and early defoliation. The pear analog of apple scab.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Dark, fuzzy olive-to-black spots appear on the leaves and the pears get rough, scabby, cracked patches. In a bad year the tree drops its leaves early.
pests.cause_seasoned: Venturia pyrina; spores overwinter in fallen leaves and infect during wet spring weather, with infection periods driven by leaf wetness and temperature. Distinct from the apple-scab fungus but managed the same way.
pests.cause_beginner: A fungus that survives winter in last year's fallen leaves and spreads in cool, wet spring weather onto the new leaves and fruit.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Apply sulfur or other labeled fungicide on a protective schedule keyed to spring infection periods; far easier to prevent than to cure once established.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Sulfur spray in spring, applied before infection takes hold, is the organic option. Once the spots are everywhere it is too late for that year, so prevention is the game.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Rake and remove fallen leaves in autumn (destroys the overwintering source), prune for airflow, and choose less-susceptible varieties.
pests.prevention_beginner: The single best move is to rake up and remove fallen leaves every autumn, that is where the fungus hides over winter. Prune for good airflow too.

diseases.name: Fire blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Blossoms and shoot tips suddenly wilt, blacken, and die, bending into a characteristic shepherd's-crook; affected branches look scorched, and sunken, oozing cankers form on wood. Asian pear is highly susceptible (20th Century and Niitaka among the worst), and a single warm, wet bloom can kill whole limbs or a young tree.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Branch tips and flower clusters suddenly turn black and look burned, as if scorched by fire, and the tip bends over into a hook. It can kill whole branches or the whole tree. Asian pears catch it easily.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Erwinia amylovora; bacteria infect through open blossoms and tender shoot tips in warm, wet spring weather and spread fastest on lush, nitrogen-pushed growth. It is the single biggest reason European pears fail in the humid South and East.
diseases.cause_beginner: Bacteria that infect through the flowers and soft new shoots in warm, wet spring weather. Fast, soft growth from too much fertilizer makes it much worse. It is the main reason pears struggle in warm, damp climates.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out infected wood at least 8 to 12 inches below visible symptoms, disinfecting tools between cuts, in dry weather; remove badly affected trees. There is no cure once established, management is prevention plus cutting it out.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut off the blackened branches well below the damage (about a hand's length past it), wiping your pruners with disinfectant between every cut so you do not spread it, and only in dry weather. There is no spray that cures it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: The decisive moves are cultivar and rootstock choice: plant more fire-blight-tolerant Asian pears (Shinko, Chojuro) on a tolerant rootstock (the OHxF series, or Pyrus calleryana). Then avoid excess nitrogen, prune only in dry weather, and follow a bloom-time forecast model where available.
diseases.prevention_beginner: The best defense is to choose a more resistant variety (Shinko, Chojuro) on a resistant rootstock, especially where summers are warm and humid. Then go easy on fertilizer (soft growth catches it) and prune only in dry weather.

diseases.name: Pear scab
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Olive to black velvety lesions on leaves and fruit that turn corky and cracked; severe infection yellows leaves and causes early defoliation and scabby, misshapen fruit.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Dark, fuzzy spots on the leaves and rough, scabby, cracked patches on the pears. In a bad year the tree drops its leaves early.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Venturia pyrina; overwinters in fallen leaves and infects during wet spring weather, infection periods set by leaf wetness and temperature.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that overwinters in last year's fallen leaves and spreads onto new leaves and fruit in cool, wet spring weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Sulfur or a labeled fungicide on a protective spring schedule keyed to infection periods; prevention beats cure.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Sulfur spray in spring before the spots appear is the organic route. Once it is widespread it is too late for that year.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rake and remove fallen leaves each autumn, prune for airflow, and choose less-susceptible varieties.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Rake up fallen leaves every fall and prune for good airflow. Resistant varieties rarely need spraying.

diseases.name: Pear decline
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Slow decline, weak growth, small leaves with reddish autumn color, and reduced yield, or in acute cases sudden collapse; driven by a phytoplasma transmitted by pear psylla and expressed through a sensitive rootstock.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The tree slowly weakens over years, with small leaves that redden early in fall and a shrinking crop, or sometimes a sudden collapse. It is tied to the pear psylla insect and to certain rootstocks.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A phytoplasma (a bacteria-like organism) spread by pear psylla; severity depends heavily on rootstock sensitivity, which is why decline-resistant rootstocks (OHxF series) matter.
diseases.cause_beginner: A tiny disease organism carried by the pear psylla insect. How badly a tree is hit depends on its rootstock, so a resistant rootstock is the main protection.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure; manage by controlling pear psylla (the vector) and, at planting, choosing a tolerant rootstock (OHxF). Remove severely declining trees.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once a tree has it. Keep pear psylla under control and, most importantly, start with a resistant rootstock when you plant.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant on a decline-tolerant rootstock (OHxF 87/97/333) and keep psylla populations low; avoid highly sensitive rootstocks.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Buy a tree grown on a resistant rootstock (the OHxF series) and keep pear psylla in check. That is the whole prevention.

pests.name: Codling moth
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Larvae tunnel into the fruit core, leaving a frass-filled entry hole (often at the calyx end) and brown trails; infested pears drop early or are inedible.
pests.symptoms_beginner: This is the classic 'worm in the fruit.' You find a small hole with brown crumbly stuff (frass) around it, and a tunnel into the core when you cut it open. Bad pears drop early.
pests.cause_seasoned: Cydia pomonella; female moths lay eggs on developing fruit and young leaves near bloom, and hatching larvae bore into the pear. Two or more generations per season in most regions. The same pest attacks apple.
pests.cause_beginner: A small moth lays eggs on the tiny pears in spring; the eggs hatch into caterpillars that crawl into the fruit. There can be two batches a summer, so the problem repeats.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Monitor with pheromone traps to time control; remove and destroy dropped and infested fruit; bag individual fruit; spinosad or kaolin clay on a degree-day/petal-fall schedule. Mating disruption works at larger scale.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick up and throw away every pear that drops, do not leave them under the tree. You can slip paper bags over young pears to keep moths out, and scent traps help you know when to act. Sprays like spinosad work if timed right.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Orchard sanitation (clear dropped fruit and debris), keep nearby abandoned pear or apple trees pruned or removed, and band trunks to catch larvae seeking pupation sites.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the ground under the tree clean of fallen pears, and wrap a band of cardboard around the trunk to trap crawling caterpillars. Nearby neglected pear or apple trees make it worse.

pests.name: Pear psylla
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Nymphs feed in clusters on shoots and leaves and exude copious sticky honeydew that blackens with sooty mold; heavy feeding causes leaf scorch, premature drop, fruit russeting, and tree decline. The signature pear pest.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves and young pears get coated in a sticky, shiny film that turns black and grimy (sooty mold), and the leaves may scorch and drop. Tiny insects cluster on the new shoots.
pests.cause_seasoned: Cacopsylla pyricola; a small psyllid specific to pear that overwinters as an adult and builds several overlapping generations through the season. Outbreaks follow broad-spectrum sprays that kill its natural enemies.
pests.cause_beginner: A tiny pear-specific insect (a kind of jumping plant louse) that sucks sap and oozes sticky stuff. It can build up fast, especially if bug sprays have wiped out the good bugs that normally keep it down.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dormant-season horticultural oil to smother overwintering adults and eggs; in-season insecticidal soap or summer oil; conserve natural enemies (anthocorid bugs, lacewings) by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides; kaolin clay deters egg-laying.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray horticultural oil while the tree is dormant in late winter to smother the overwintering insects, and use insecticidal soap in the growing season. Avoid harsh sprays, which kill the helpful bugs that eat psylla.
pests.prevention_seasoned: A well-timed dormant oil program plus a natural-enemy-friendly spray regime is the backbone of psylla management; avoid the lush nitrogen-pushed growth psylla favors.
pests.prevention_beginner: A good dormant oil spray in late winter and going easy on harsh sprays and fertilizer keep this pear-specific pest in check.

pests.name: Pear scab
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Olive-green to black velvety spots on leaves, shoots, and fruit; fruit lesions become corky and cracked, and severe infection causes leaf yellowing and early defoliation. The pear analog of apple scab.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Dark, fuzzy olive-to-black spots appear on the leaves and the pears get rough, scabby, cracked patches. In a bad year the tree drops its leaves early.
pests.cause_seasoned: Venturia pyrina; spores overwinter in fallen leaves and infect during wet spring weather, with infection periods driven by leaf wetness and temperature. Distinct from the apple-scab fungus but managed the same way.
pests.cause_beginner: A fungus that survives winter in last year's fallen leaves and spreads in cool, wet spring weather onto the new leaves and fruit.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Apply sulfur or other labeled fungicide on a protective schedule keyed to spring infection periods; far easier to prevent than to cure once established.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Sulfur spray in spring, applied before infection takes hold, is the organic option. Once the spots are everywhere it is too late for that year, so prevention is the game.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Rake and remove fallen leaves in autumn (destroys the overwintering source), prune for airflow, and choose less-susceptible varieties.
pests.prevention_beginner: The single best move is to rake up and remove fallen leaves every autumn, that is where the fungus hides over winter. Prune for good airflow too.

pests.name: Fabraea leaf spot
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Numerous small, dark purple-to-black spots on leaves and fruit through summer; heavy infection causes blotching, early defoliation, and pitted, cracked fruit. Most damaging in warm, humid regions and on susceptible cultivars (Bartlett, Bosc).
pests.symptoms_beginner: Lots of small dark spots speckle the leaves in mid to late summer, and the tree may drop a lot of leaves early. The pears can get spotted and pitted too.
pests.cause_seasoned: Entomosporium mespili (Fabraea maculata); the fungus overwinters in fallen leaves and infected twigs and spreads in warm, rainy summer weather, building late in the season.
pests.cause_beginner: A fungus that lives in old fallen leaves and spreads in warm, rainy summer weather, getting worse as summer goes on. It is a bigger problem in hot, humid areas.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protective fungicide (labeled product) on a summer schedule where it has a history; rake and destroy fallen leaves to cut the overwintering source.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: If your tree gets this every year, a protective fungicide through summer helps. Always rake up and remove the fallen leaves to break the cycle.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Fall leaf removal, airflow pruning, and resistant cultivar choice; the disease is far worse in the humid Southeast than in arid or northern regions.
pests.prevention_beginner: Rake up fallen leaves every fall, prune so air moves through the tree, and in hot humid areas choose a resistant variety.

diseases.name: Fire blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Blossoms and shoot tips suddenly wilt, blacken, and die, bending into a characteristic 'shepherd's crook'; affected branches look scorched, and sunken, oozing cankers form on wood. Pear is markedly MORE susceptible than apple, and a single warm, wet bloom can kill whole limbs or a young tree.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Branch tips and flower clusters suddenly turn black and look burned, as if scorched by fire, and the tip bends over into a hook shape. It can kill whole branches or the whole tree. Pears catch it worse than apples.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Erwinia amylovora; bacteria infect through open blossoms and tender shoot tips in warm, wet spring weather and spread fastest on lush, nitrogen-pushed growth. It is the single biggest reason European pears fail in the humid South and East.
diseases.cause_beginner: Bacteria that infect through the flowers and soft new shoots in warm, wet spring weather. Fast, soft growth from too much fertilizer makes it much worse. It is the main reason pears struggle in warm, damp climates.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out infected wood at least 8 to 12 inches below visible symptoms, disinfecting tools between cuts, in dry weather; remove badly affected trees. There is no cure once established, management is prevention plus cutting it out.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut off the blackened branches well below the damage (about a hand's length past it), wiping your pruners with disinfectant between every cut so you do not spread it, and only in dry weather. There is no spray that cures it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: The decisive move is variety and rootstock choice: plant fire-blight-resistant cultivars (Kieffer, Orient, Moonglow, Ayers, Warren, Magness) on a tolerant rootstock (the OHxF series). Then avoid excess nitrogen, prune only in dry weather, and follow a bloom-time forecast model where available.
diseases.prevention_beginner: The best defense is to choose a resistant variety (Kieffer, Orient, Moonglow, Ayers, Warren) on a resistant rootstock, especially where summers are warm and humid. Then go easy on fertilizer (soft growth catches it) and prune only in dry weather.

diseases.name: Pear scab
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Olive to black velvety lesions on leaves and fruit that turn corky and cracked; severe infection yellows leaves and causes early defoliation and scabby, misshapen fruit.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Dark, fuzzy spots on the leaves and rough, scabby, cracked patches on the pears. In a bad year the tree drops its leaves early.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Venturia pyrina; overwinters in fallen leaves and infects during wet spring weather, infection periods set by leaf wetness and temperature.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that overwinters in last year's fallen leaves and spreads onto new leaves and fruit in cool, wet spring weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Sulfur or a labeled fungicide on a protective spring schedule keyed to infection periods; prevention beats cure.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Sulfur spray in spring before the spots appear is the organic route. Once it is widespread it is too late for that year.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rake and remove fallen leaves each autumn, prune for airflow, and choose less-susceptible varieties.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Rake up fallen leaves every fall and prune for good airflow. Resistant varieties rarely need spraying.

diseases.name: Fabraea leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Many small dark purple-black spots on leaves and fruit through summer, leading to early defoliation and pitted, cracked fruit; the dominant summer foliar disease of pear in warm, humid regions.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Lots of small dark spots cover the leaves in summer, and the tree can drop most of its leaves early. The pears get spotted and pitted.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Entomosporium mespili; overwinters in fallen leaves and twig lesions and spreads in warm, rainy summer weather, intensifying late in the season.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that lives in old leaves and twigs and spreads in warm, rainy summer weather, getting worse through the summer.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Protective fungicide on a summer schedule where it recurs; rigorous fall leaf removal to cut the overwintering inoculum.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: A protective fungicide through summer if it keeps coming back, plus raking up all the fallen leaves in fall.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Fall sanitation, airflow pruning, and resistant cultivars; far less of a problem in arid and northern climates.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Rake up fallen leaves, prune for airflow, and pick a resistant variety in hot, humid areas.

diseases.name: Pear decline
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Slow decline, weak growth, small leaves with reddish autumn color, and reduced yield, or in acute cases sudden collapse; driven by a phytoplasma transmitted by pear psylla and expressed through a sensitive rootstock.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The tree slowly weakens over years, with small leaves that redden early in fall and a shrinking crop, or sometimes a sudden collapse. It is tied to the pear psylla insect and to certain rootstocks.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A phytoplasma (a bacteria-like organism) spread by pear psylla; severity depends heavily on rootstock sensitivity, which is why decline-resistant rootstocks (OHxF series) matter.
diseases.cause_beginner: A tiny disease organism carried by the pear psylla insect. How badly a tree is hit depends on its rootstock, so a resistant rootstock is the main protection.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure; manage by controlling pear psylla (the vector) and, at planting, choosing a tolerant rootstock (OHxF). Remove severely declining trees.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once a tree has it. Keep pear psylla under control and, most importantly, start with a resistant rootstock when you plant.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant on a decline-tolerant rootstock (OHxF 87/97/333) and keep psylla populations low; avoid highly sensitive rootstocks.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Buy a tree grown on a resistant rootstock (the OHxF series) and keep pear psylla in check. That is the whole prevention.

pests.name: Scale insects
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small, immobile bumps on bark, twigs, and the underside of leaves; white peach scale shows as snow-white encrustations on the trunk and limbs, while soft scales are brown and rounded. Heavy infestations produce sticky honeydew that blackens with sooty mold and draws ants. Vigor and fruit quality decline where scale builds up unchecked.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Little bumps stuck to the bark, twigs, and leaf undersides that do not move. White peach scale looks like snow-white crust on the trunk and branches; other scales are small brown domes. They leave a sticky coating (honeydew) that turns black with sooty mold and attracts ants. Bad cases slowly weaken the tree.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several scale species, notably white peach scale and soft scales (Parthenolecanium spp.), which insert their mouthparts and feed on sap under a protective waxy shell. Their honeydew supports sooty mold. Populations flare where natural enemies have been knocked back by broad-spectrum sprays.
pests.cause_beginner: Tiny sap-sucking insects that hide under a waxy shell, mainly white peach scale and soft scales. They feed on the tree's sap and drip sticky honeydew that grows black mold. They get worse when sprays kill off the helpful insects that normally eat them.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Preserve natural enemies (ladybugs, parasitic wasps) by not spraying broadly, since they usually hold scale to tolerable levels on persimmon. Prune out and destroy heavily encrusted wood. A dormant-season horticultural oil application smothers overwintering scale on the bark and is the main direct control for a backyard tree.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Let the helpful bugs do the work by avoiding broad sprays, since ladybugs and tiny wasps usually keep scale in check on persimmon. Cut out and throw away badly crusted branches. A spray of horticultural oil while the tree is leafless in winter smothers the scale on the bark and is the simplest hands-on control.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep the tree vigorous, avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that disrupt biological control, and monitor the trunk and scaffolds for early white encrustations so a dormant oil can be timed before populations explode.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the tree healthy, skip the broad bug sprays that kill the good insects, and check the trunk and branches now and then for the first white crusty patches so you can put on a winter oil spray before it spreads.

pests.name: Mealybugs
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Soft, oval insects coated in white, cottony wax clustered in leaf axils, under the calyx of the fruit, and along shoots. Like scale, they excrete honeydew that fosters sooty mold and ants, and feeding under the calyx can contaminate and blemish fruit.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Small soft insects covered in white, cottony fluff, tucked into leaf joints, under the leafy cap of the fruit, and along stems. They leave the same sticky honeydew and black mold as scale, and where they hide under the fruit's cap they can spoil its look.
pests.cause_seasoned: Mealybugs (several species) that suck phloem sap and shelter in protected crevices, including beneath the fruit calyx. Ant-tended colonies persist because ants protect them from natural enemies for the honeydew.
pests.cause_beginner: Sap-sucking insects called mealybugs that hide in sheltered spots, including under the leafy cap on the fruit. Ants often protect them because they want the sweet honeydew, which lets the mealybugs build up.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rely first on natural enemies, which generally keep mealybugs below damaging levels on landscape fruit trees; avoid the broad-spectrum sprays that disrupt them. Control honeydew-farming ants (sticky trunk bands) so predators can work. Spot-treat visible colonies with a horticultural oil or insecticidal soap.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Let natural predators handle most mealybugs, and avoid broad sprays that kill those helpers. Stop ants from climbing the trunk with a sticky band so the predators can reach the mealybugs. Dab visible clusters with horticultural oil or insecticidal soap.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Maintain biological control by minimizing broad-spectrum sprays, manage ants, and inspect the calyx end of developing fruit where mealybugs hide, removing infested fruit early.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the helpful insects around by not spraying broadly, keep ants off the tree, and check under the cap of the growing fruit where mealybugs like to hide, picking off any infested ones early.

pests.name: Persimmon psyllid
pests.symptoms_seasoned: New leaves curl, roll, and cup around the feeding of tiny nymphs in spring, often distorting the flush of young growth. Small crawlers and their waxy filaments may be visible inside the rolled leaves. Damage is largely cosmetic on an established tree but can stunt young shoots.
pests.symptoms_beginner: In spring the new leaves curl and roll up around tiny insects feeding inside. You may see small crawlers and white waxy threads inside the rolled leaves. On an older tree the harm is mostly cosmetic, but it can slow down a young one.
pests.cause_seasoned: The persimmon psyllid, a small sap-feeding insect whose nymphs feed on expanding leaves in spring and induce the characteristic leaf roll. It is a minor, mostly cosmetic pest of both native and Oriental persimmon.
pests.cause_beginner: A small sap-feeding insect called the persimmon psyllid. Its young feed on the new spring leaves and make them curl. It is a minor pest that mostly just looks bad.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Usually no treatment is warranted; natural enemies and the tree's vigor absorb the damage. On a small tree, prune off and destroy the worst rolled tips in spring. Preserve beneficial insects by avoiding broad sprays.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Usually nothing needs to be done, since the tree shrugs it off. On a small tree you can clip off the worst curled tips in spring. Avoid broad sprays so the helpful insects stay around.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Little is required. Keeping the tree healthy and preserving natural enemies keeps the psyllid a cosmetic nuisance rather than a problem.
pests.prevention_beginner: There is not much to do. A healthy tree with its natural predators intact keeps this pest to a harmless nuisance.

pests.name: Persimmon borer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Wilting or dying shoots and, on the trunk, gummy ooze mixed with sawdust-like frass near the base where larvae tunnel the inner bark. Young trees can be girdled and killed; it is the one persimmon pest extension warns can be serious, particularly in the Southeast.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Shoots that wilt or die, and near the bottom of the trunk a sticky ooze mixed with what looks like sawdust, where the larvae are tunneling under the bark. A young tree can be ringed and killed, so this is the one persimmon pest to take seriously.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of the persimmon (and flatheaded) borers that bore into the lower trunk and inner bark. Trees stressed by wounds or drought are attacked first, but healthy bark can also be entered; it affects both native and Oriental persimmon.
pests.cause_beginner: The larvae (grub stage) of borer beetles and moths that tunnel into the lower trunk. Wounded or stressed trees are hit hardest, but a healthy tree can be attacked too.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: No spray reaches larvae already inside the trunk. Expose the crown, locate entry holes by the gum and frass, and kill larvae by hand with a wire. Keep the trunk base free of mechanical wounds and remove badly infested young wood.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the larvae are inside, no spray reaches them. Scrape soil away from the base, find the holes marked by gum and sawdust, and kill the grubs with a stiff wire. Keep mowers and trimmers away from the trunk so you are not giving the borers wounds to enter.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Protect the lower trunk from injury, keep the tree vigorous and well watered, and inspect the trunk base each late summer for fresh gum and frass so an infestation is caught in its first year.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep mowers and string trimmers off the trunk, keep the tree healthy and watered, and check the base of the trunk each late summer for fresh ooze and sawdust so you catch borers early.

diseases.name: Anthracnose
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark, sunken lesions on fruit, and spots and dieback on leaves and young shoots, most damaging in warm, wet weather and humid regions. Infected fruit can rot before or after harvest, and severe leaf infection thins the canopy.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Dark, sunken spots on the fruit and spots or dieback on leaves and new shoots, worst in warm, rainy weather. Bad cases rot the fruit and thin out the leaves.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Anthracnose fungi (Colletotrichum and related genera) that overwinter in dead wood and mummified fruit and spread by rain-splash in warm, humid conditions. Pressure is highest in the wet Southeast and lowest in dry-summer climates.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus (anthracnose) that survives winter in dead wood and old fruit and spreads in warm, wet weather. It is a bigger problem in humid, rainy areas than in dry ones.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Sanitation is the core control: prune out and destroy dead and cankered wood and remove mummified fruit, and keep the canopy open so it dries quickly after rain. Remove and dispose of infected fruit promptly. Fungicides are rarely needed on a backyard tree if sanitation is kept up.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cleanup is the main fix: cut out dead branches, pick off and throw away any shriveled old fruit, and prune so the tree is open and dries fast after rain. Remove spotted fruit as you see it. A home tree rarely needs spraying if you keep it clean.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Choose an open canopy through pruning, clear fallen and mummified fruit each season, and site the tree with good air movement. In high-pressure humid regions, favor cultivars with better tolerance.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep the tree open with light pruning, clean up fallen and dried-up fruit every year, and plant it where air moves freely. In rainy areas, pick a variety known to hold up better.

diseases.name: Root and crown rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: General decline, sparse yellowing foliage, and dieback on a tree in heavy or poorly drained soil, with dark, decayed bark and roots at and below the soil line. Asian persimmon is especially susceptible; the tree may collapse over a season or two once the crown is girdled.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A tree that slowly goes downhill, with thin yellow leaves and dying branches, usually in wet or heavy soil. The bark and roots at the base turn dark and rotten. Asian persimmon is especially prone, and a badly affected tree can die within a year or two.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne Phytophthora (and related) fungi that attack roots and the crown in waterlogged soil. Oriental persimmon is notably susceptible to root rot, which is a chief reason it is often grafted onto the more tolerant native (D. virginiana) rootstock.
diseases.cause_beginner: Water-mold fungi in the soil (Phytophthora) that rot the roots and crown when the ground stays wet. Asian persimmon is easily hit, which is why it is often grafted onto the tougher native persimmon roots.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once the crown is rotting. Management is prevention through drainage: never plant in standing-water sites, plant on a mound in heavy soil, and choose a tree on tolerant native rootstock where drainage is marginal. Avoid overwatering an established tree.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the base is rotting there is no fixing it, so this one is all about prevention. Never plant where water stands, plant on a raised mound in heavy soil, and pick a tree grafted onto native persimmon roots if your drainage is iffy. Do not overwater an older tree.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant only on well-drained ground or a raised berm, select tolerant (native) rootstock in marginal soils, and water deeply but infrequently rather than keeping the root zone saturated.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant only where water drains well, or on a raised mound, choose a tree on native persimmon rootstock if your soil is heavy, and water deeply now and then instead of keeping the soil soggy.

diseases.name: Leaf spot and twig dieback
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Circular to angular leaf spots that may yellow and drop leaves in a wet season, and dieback of small twigs. Usually a minor, cosmetic issue on an otherwise healthy persimmon, which extension sources note has few serious disease problems.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Round or angular spots on the leaves that can turn them yellow and drop in a wet year, plus a little dieback of small twigs. On a healthy persimmon this is usually minor and just cosmetic.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Several leaf-spot fungi favored by prolonged leaf wetness. Persimmon is generally regarded as having no serious insect or disease problems, so leaf spot is typically a low-impact, weather-driven nuisance.
diseases.cause_beginner: Common leaf-spot fungi that show up when leaves stay wet a long time. Persimmon has few real disease problems, so this is usually just a minor, weather-related annoyance.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rake and remove fallen infected leaves to reduce carryover, keep the canopy open, and keep the tree vigorous; fungicides are seldom justified on a home tree.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Rake up and remove fallen spotted leaves, keep the tree open, and keep it healthy. A home tree almost never needs a spray for this.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Good air movement, an open canopy, and fall leaf cleanup keep leaf spot to a cosmetic level.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Good airflow, light pruning to keep the tree open, and cleaning up fallen leaves in autumn keep this to a harmless level.

pests.name: Leaf-footed bug
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Often no external mark on the fruit at all; the damage is inside. Cut a fed-on fruit and you find brown spots on the inner rind where the insect's needlelike mouthpart pierced, and arils that have darkened, withered, or turned corky. Late-season feeding as fruit ripens is the worst, and it opens the door to internal fungal rots.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Usually you see nothing wrong on the outside of the fruit, because the damage is inside. If you cut a fruit open, you find brown spots on the inner skin and seeds (arils) that have gone dark, shriveled, or corky. It is worst late in the season as the fruit ripens, and it can let rot start inside.
pests.cause_seasoned: The leaf-footed bug (Leptoglossus species), a large brown true bug with flattened, leaf-like flares on its hind legs. Adults and nymphs pierce fruit to feed; on pomegranate their feeding can introduce yeasts and fungal spores that discolor and rot the arils. They overwinter as adults in sheltered aggregations and move onto fruit as it develops.
pests.cause_beginner: A big brown bug called the leaf-footed bug, named for the little leaf-shaped flares on its back legs. It and its young pierce the fruit to feed, and that can carry in yeasts and fungi that discolor and rot the seeds inside. The adults spend winter hidden in sheltered groups, then move onto the fruit as it forms.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no easy rescue spray for a backyard plant. The practical controls are physical: hand-pick or knock adults and nymphs into soapy water in the cool early morning when they are sluggish, clear the weedy and sheltered spots where they overwinter and aggregate, and bag developing fruit clusters in mesh where feasible. Encourage the natural egg parasites and general predators by keeping insectary flowers nearby.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: For a backyard plant, the best fixes are hands-on: in the cool early morning, knock the bugs into a bucket of soapy water, and clean up the weedy, sheltered places where they spend the winter and gather. Where you can, cover fruit clusters with fine mesh bags. Flowers nearby that bring in helpful insects also keep numbers down.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Monitor from fruit set onward, since the internal damage is invisible until you cut the fruit. Keep the area weed-free to remove overwintering and breeding habitat, and watch for the adults congregating in spring. Early detection and hand-removal before populations build is the most effective home strategy.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep an eye out from the time fruit forms, because you cannot see the damage from outside until you cut a fruit open. Keep weeds cleared to take away the places the bugs hide and breed, and look for the adults gathering in spring. Catching and removing them early, before there are many, works best.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects on new shoots, leaf undersides, and flower stems, with sticky honeydew, sooty black mold on leaves and fruit, curled or distorted new growth, and attending ants.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Groups of tiny soft insects on new shoots and the undersides of leaves, leaving a sticky coating (honeydew) that turns into black sooty mold, plus curled new leaves and ants running up and down the plant.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species colonize tender pomegranate growth in spring, multiplying fast in warm weather. Their honeydew supports sooty mold and draws ants, which protect the aphids from predators.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids, tiny sap-sucking insects that build up on soft new growth in spring. They multiply quickly, and the sticky honeydew they leave grows black mold and attracts ants that guard them.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: A strong jet of water knocks aphids off and is often enough on an established plant. Preserve natural enemies (ladybugs, lacewings, syrphid larvae) by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays; insecticidal soap or horticultural oil handles heavier infestations. Control ants, which farm aphids, to let predators work.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spraying the plant with a strong stream of water knocks most aphids off and is often all an established plant needs. Let the good bugs (ladybugs, lacewings) do their job by avoiding harsh sprays; insecticidal soap helps if there are a lot. Keeping ants off the plant lets the helpful insects control them.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep nitrogen feeding moderate, since lush growth pushed by excess nitrogen draws aphids. Support beneficial insects with nearby flowers, and manage ants so predators are not chased off.
pests.prevention_beginner: Do not overfeed with nitrogen, because all that soft new growth attracts aphids. Grow flowers nearby to bring in helpful insects, and keep ants away so those helpers can do their work.

pests.name: Whitefly
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny white moth-like insects that fly up in clouds when the plant is disturbed, gathered on leaf undersides with their pale nymphs; honeydew and sooty mold follow, and heavy infestations yellow and weaken leaves.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Tiny white insects like little moths that flutter up when you brush the plant, sitting under the leaves along with their flat, pale young. They leave sticky honeydew and black sooty mold, and a lot of them yellow the leaves.
pests.cause_seasoned: Whiteflies, small sap-feeding insects that colonize leaf undersides and reproduce rapidly in warm weather. Like aphids, they excrete honeydew that fosters sooty mold.
pests.cause_beginner: Whiteflies, small sap-sucking insects that live under the leaves and multiply fast in warm weather. Like aphids, they leave honeydew that grows sooty mold.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hose off foliage and rely on natural enemies (lacewings, ladybugs, parasitic wasps), which usually keep whiteflies in check on an outdoor plant. Insecticidal soap or horticultural oil on leaf undersides helps in heavy cases; yellow sticky traps monitor and reduce adults.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the leaves with water and let helpful insects do most of the work; they usually keep whiteflies under control outdoors. Insecticidal soap sprayed under the leaves helps if there are many, and yellow sticky cards catch the adults.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep plants healthy and avoid excess nitrogen and dusty, stressed conditions that favor whitefly buildup. Preserve natural enemies by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the plant healthy, avoid overfeeding with nitrogen, and do not let it get dusty and stressed, which whiteflies like. Avoid harsh sprays so the helpful insects survive.

pests.name: Mealybugs and scale
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Cottony white tufts (mealybugs) in leaf axils, branch crotches, and inside the fruit calyx (crown), or small immobile brown or waxy bumps (scale) on stems and leaves; both produce honeydew and sooty mold, and mealybugs hidden in the crown can contaminate the fruit interior.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Fuzzy white cottony spots (mealybugs) tucked into branch joints and inside the crown of the fruit, or small hard brown bumps (scale) stuck to stems and leaves. Both leave sticky honeydew and black mold, and mealybugs hiding in the fruit crown can get inside the fruit.
pests.cause_seasoned: Mealybugs and various scale insects, slow-moving or immobile sap feeders that shelter in protected spots including the fruit's crown. Ants tend and spread them, and their honeydew fuels sooty mold.
pests.cause_beginner: Mealybugs and scale insects, sap-sucking pests that hide in sheltered spots, including the crown of the fruit. Ants move them around and protect them, and their honeydew grows black mold.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spot-treat with horticultural oil or insecticidal soap, dab visible mealybug colonies with an alcohol-dipped swab, and prune out heavily infested wood. Control ants to let natural enemies (including mealybug destroyers and parasitic wasps) suppress them. Remove fruit with infested crowns.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Wipe visible mealybugs with a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol, spray with horticultural oil or insecticidal soap, and cut out badly infested branches. Keep ants off so the helpful insects can work, and throw away any fruit with bugs packed into the crown.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep ants under control, avoid excess nitrogen, and inspect the fruit crown and branch crotches where these pests hide. Good airflow and light through the canopy discourage them.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep ants away, do not overfeed, and check the fruit crowns and branch joints where these pests hide. An open, airy plant with good light bothers them.

diseases.name: Alternaria heart rot (black heart)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: The fruit looks nearly normal outside, perhaps a little light in weight or slightly off-color (a paler red), while the interior rots: arils turn brown and mushy and a black mold sporulates inside. There is often no external cue, so the rot is discovered only on cutting.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: From the outside the fruit looks almost fine, maybe a bit light or a paler red, but inside it is rotting: the seeds turn brown and mushy with black mold. There is usually no sign on the outside, so you only find it when you cut the fruit open.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Alternaria (and related molds) infects through the open flower during rainy or humid bloom weather and grows silently inside the developing fruit. Insect and bird punctures (notably leaf-footed bug feeding) give it a second way in. Wet weather at and after bloom is the main driver, which is why it is a bigger problem in humid climates.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus called Alternaria gets into the fruit through the open flower in damp, rainy bloom weather and grows quietly inside. Wounds from insects (like the leaf-footed bug) or birds let it in too. Wet weather around bloom is the main cause, so it is worse in humid areas.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once the inside is rotting; the fruit is lost. Control is preventive: it is far less of a problem in hot, dry climates, so the main levers are managing leaf-footed bug and other fruit-piercing pests, keeping the canopy open and airy, and removing and destroying infected and mummified fruit so spores do not carry over.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Once a fruit is rotting inside, it cannot be saved. The way to fight it is to prevent it: it is much less of a problem in hot, dry weather, so keep the leaf-footed bug and other fruit-piercing pests under control, keep the plant open and airy, and pick off and throw away any rotted or old dried fruit so the mold does not spread to next year.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Favor dry-climate siting, open canopies, and drip (not overhead) watering to keep bloom and fruit dry. Control fruit-piercing insects, sanitize by removing mummies and rotted fruit, and, in humid regions, expect this to be a limiting disease and choose the most open, breezy sites.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Grow it where summers are hot and dry if you can, keep the plant open, and water at the ground rather than over the top. Keep fruit-piercing bugs in check, clean up rotted and old dried fruit, and know that in humid, rainy areas this disease may limit your crop, so pick the most open, breezy spot.

diseases.name: Botrytis gray mold / fruit rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Fuzzy gray-brown mold on flowers, on fruit (often starting at the crown or a wound), and on stored fruit; soft brown rot spreads in cool, wet, or humid conditions and in storage, and can move between touching fruit.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Fuzzy gray-brown mold on the flowers and fruit, often starting at the crown end or a wound, with soft brown rot that spreads in cool, damp weather and in storage. It can spread from one fruit to another where they touch.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Botrytis cinerea (gray mold), which infects flowers and wounded or overripe fruit in cool, wet, humid conditions. It overwinters on plant debris and old fruit and is a common cause of post-harvest rot.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus called Botrytis, or gray mold, that infects flowers and damaged or overripe fruit in cool, damp weather. It survives on old fruit and plant litter and is a common cause of rot in stored fruit.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy moldy flowers, fruit, and debris promptly. Keep the canopy open and dry, harvest before rains, handle fruit gently to avoid wounds, and refrigerate sound fruit quickly, since cold storage slows the mold. There is no home spray cure once fruit is rotting.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off and throw away moldy flowers, fruit, and litter right away. Keep the plant open and dry, pick before the rains, handle fruit gently so it does not bruise, and refrigerate good fruit soon, since cold slows the mold. Once a fruit is rotting there is no home spray that fixes it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Prioritize air circulation and dry foliage: open pruning, root-zone watering, prompt sanitation of old fruit and debris, and gentle handling with quick cooling at harvest. Cull split and wounded fruit, which are entry points.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep the plant open and the leaves dry: prune for airflow, water at the ground, clean up old fruit and litter, and handle and chill fruit carefully at harvest. Remove split or damaged fruit, which is where the mold gets in.

diseases.name: Cercospora fruit and leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small dark spots and blotches on fruit and leaves that enlarge and merge; heavily spotted fruit is russeted and downgraded, and severe leaf infection causes yellowing and drop. Most common and damaging in warm, humid, rainy climates.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small dark spots on the fruit and leaves that grow and run together; badly spotted fruit looks rough and russeted, and heavy leaf spotting yellows the leaves and drops them. It is worst in warm, humid, rainy areas.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The fungus Cercospora punicae (with related fungi such as Colletotrichum and Botryosphaeria in the same wet climates). It thrives on prolonged leaf and fruit wetness, so it is a leading reason pomegranate fruits poorly in the humid Southeast and other rainy regions.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus (Cercospora punicae, along with related fungi in the same wet climates) that spreads when leaves and fruit stay wet for a long time. It is a big reason pomegranate does poorly in the humid Southeast and other rainy places.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Home control is limited and preventive: choose an open, sunny, breezy site so foliage dries fast, prune for airflow, water at the ground, and remove fallen leaves and infected fruit. In consistently humid, rainy climates, expect this disease to cap fruit quality regardless of care.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no easy home cure, so prevention matters: plant in an open, sunny, breezy spot so the leaves dry quickly, prune to open the plant, water at the ground, and clean up fallen leaves and spotted fruit. In damp, rainy climates this disease will likely limit your fruit quality no matter what.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Site selection is the main defense: open, sloped, breezy ground with strong air movement, especially at bloom. Wide spacing, open canopies, ground-level irrigation, and sanitation of fallen debris reduce pressure. In hot, dry climates it is a minor issue.
diseases.prevention_beginner: The best defense is where and how you plant it: an open, breezy, sloped spot with good air movement, wide spacing, an open plant, watering at the ground, and cleaning up fallen leaves and fruit. In hot, dry climates it is barely a problem.
